title: My Kneecap Slipped Out of Place: Will It Happen Again, and Do I Need MPFL Surgery?
seoTitle: Kneecap Dislocation: Will It Recur? Do You Need MPFL Surgery?
metaDescription: First kneecap dislocation? What gets damaged, who is likely to dislocate again, why most start with rehab, and when MPFL surgery is worth discussing.
intro: A kneecap that suddenly shifts out of place is frightening, especially when it happens to a teenager during football, kabaddi or a dance class. Often it slides back on its own, and the family is left with a swollen knee and two questions: will it happen again, and does my child need an operation? The honest answers depend on the shape of the knee, the person's age and what the scan shows, and for many first-time dislocations the answer to the second question is no.
summary: After a first kneecap dislocation, most people start with physiotherapy and a short period of bracing, not surgery. Roughly one-third of adults dislocate again, and the risk is higher in younger patients and in knees with a shallow groove or a high-riding kneecap. MPFL reconstruction is usually considered for repeated dislocations, high-risk anatomy, or a loose fragment.

sections.heading: What actually happens when the kneecap dislocates?
sections.body:
In almost every case the kneecap slips outwards, towards the outer side of the knee, usually during a twist with the foot planted. On its way out it stretches or tears the medial patellofemoral ligament (MPFL), a band on the inner side that, as AAOS OrthoInfo describes, stops the kneecap moving too far sideways. It can also chip cartilage or bone.

Many kneecaps pop back in by themselves when the leg is straightened. Even then, the knee usually swells quickly because of bleeding inside the joint. An X-ray checks for fractures, and an MRI is often advised to look at the MPFL and for loose fragments of bone or cartilage.

sections.heading: Will it happen again?
sections.body:
It might, but it is not inevitable. A 2019 review in Sports Medicine and Arthroscopy Review reports that approximately one-third of skeletally mature patients go on to have recurrent instability after a first dislocation. In children and young teenagers whose bones are still growing, and in knees with certain shapes, the chance is higher.

AAOS OrthoInfo notes that non-surgical treatment of a first-time dislocation often gives good outcomes with a relatively low recurrence rate, but that some patients are at higher risk and should discuss this with their doctor. The factors below are the ones that same review lists as raising the risk. Several of them can be judged from X-rays and MRI, which is why imaging matters even when the knee looks better.

The groove at the end of the thighbone, where the kneecap runs, is shallow or flat
The kneecap sits higher than usual, so it engages the groove later as the knee bends
The bump on the shinbone where the kneecap tendon attaches sits too far to the outer side, pulling the kneecap outwards

sections.heading: Is surgery better than rehab after a first dislocation?
sections.body:
Nobody can say for certain yet. A 2023 Cochrane review of 10 trials with 519 participants concluded that it is uncertain whether surgery lowers the risk of another dislocation, because the evidence is of very low certainty. So for most first-time dislocations without a fragment, starting with rehabilitation remains reasonable.

In that review the illustrative figure was about 348 per 1,000 people re-dislocating after non-surgical care, with an estimated 157 fewer per 1,000 after surgery. The trials were small, varied and mostly used older operations, so these numbers should be taken as a rough signal, not a promise.

Rehab usually means a short time in a brace and on crutches, followed by physiotherapy that strengthens the thigh and hip muscles. AAOS OrthoInfo describes the goal of non-surgical care as a return to normal activities within one to three months.

sections.heading: When is MPFL reconstruction, with or without a tibial tubercle osteotomy, considered?
sections.body:
AAOS OrthoInfo says surgery is typically reserved for very high-risk first-time dislocations, recurrent instability, or a kneecap that tracks badly out of position. A loose fragment of bone or cartilage that needs fixing or removing is another common reason to operate early, sometimes by keyhole surgery.

MPFL reconstruction replaces the torn ligament with a tendon graft, rebuilding the inner restraint. When the bony shape is part of the problem, the MPFL alone may not be enough. A tibial tubercle osteotomy cuts and moves the bony bump on the shinbone to realign the pull on the kneecap or to bring a high kneecap down. The review above describes this as an increasingly 'a la carte' approach: each procedure is matched to the risk factors a particular knee has. In children who are still growing, the technique is adapted to protect the growth plates.

sections.heading: What is recovery like, and when can I return to sport?
sections.body:
With rehab alone, the OrthoInfo goal is normal daily activity within one to three months, with demanding sport often taking longer. After MPFL reconstruction, recovery is slower and staged: protected walking, regaining full bend, then strength, then running and sport-specific drills. Timelines vary with the procedure and should be set by your own surgeon.

The test for returning to sport is not the calendar alone. The knee should have full movement, near-equal strength to the other side, no swelling after training, and the person should feel confident pivoting and landing. AAOS OrthoInfo reports a re-dislocation rate of less than 10% after stabilising procedures, which is lower than after rehab alone but not zero.

sections.heading: What are the warning signs that need prompt review?
sections.body: See an orthopaedic surgeon soon if the knee swells heavily within hours, if you cannot straighten it fully, or if it locks or catches. These can mean a piece of cartilage or bone has broken off and is floating in the joint. That loose body is one of the few situations where early surgery after a first dislocation is usually discussed.
bullets: The kneecap stays out of place and does not slide back in: go to an emergency department and do not try to force it
The knee is locked and cannot be straightened
Large, rapid, tense swelling after the injury
Unable to put weight on the leg, or a clear bony tender spot
Repeated giving-way episodes after a first dislocation

faqs.q: Does every kneecap dislocation need MPFL surgery?
faqs.a: No. Most first-time dislocations without a loose fragment are treated with bracing and physiotherapy. A 2023 Cochrane review found the evidence that early surgery prevents repeat dislocation is very low certainty. Surgery is usually discussed for repeated dislocations, high-risk knee shape, or a loose piece of bone or cartilage.

faqs.q: What is the chance it will happen again?
faqs.a: A 2019 review reports that about one-third of adults with a first dislocation have further instability. The chance is higher in younger patients and in knees with a shallow groove (trochlear dysplasia), a high kneecap (patella alta), or an outward-placed shinbone attachment.

faqs.q: Why is an MRI needed if the kneecap went back in?
faqs.a: Because the main concerns are not always visible from outside. An MRI shows whether the MPFL is torn and whether a piece of cartilage or bone has broken off. A loose fragment may need surgery, and the scan also helps judge the knee shape that affects recurrence risk.

faqs.q: How long before my child can play sport again?
faqs.a: With rehab alone, AAOS OrthoInfo describes a goal of returning to normal activities within one to three months, with demanding sport sometimes taking longer. After surgery it is slower. Return should depend on full movement, good strength and confidence, not just time.

faqs.q: What is a tibial tubercle osteotomy?
faqs.a: It is an operation that moves the bony bump on the shinbone where the kneecap tendon attaches, to correct the pull on the kneecap or bring a high kneecap down. It is sometimes combined with MPFL reconstruction when the bone shape is part of the problem.
